h: Beat the clock, then see the city
p: If you're new to escape rooms, the secret is simple: keep talking. Most groups who fall short aren't lacking brains, they're lacking communication. Shout out every number, symbol and strange object you find, put solved items aside so you don't keep picking them up, and agree who will ask for a hint if you're properly stuck. Glasgow groups are rarely short of chat, so you're already halfway there.

Pick your room with your group in mind. Some themes lean spooky, others are more adventure-led, so a quick look at the options before you book helps everyone enjoy it. For birthdays and nights out, an early-evening slot leaves plenty of time for dinner afterwards. And if anyone in your group is claustrophobic or has access needs, have a word with the team when booking so they can point you to the right room.

There's a lot to pair it with in the city centre. A short walk up Buchanan Street brings you to Royal Exchange Square and the Gallery of Modern Art, famous for the Duke of Wellington statue outside with a traffic cone on his head. George Square, the city's grand civic heart, is just beyond, and the Merchant City's streets of restaurants, bars and independent shops are on the doorstep. The Barras market in the East End is worth a weekend wander, while the subway from St Enoch can whisk you out west to Kelvinhall for Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, one of the city's most-loved buildings, with Kelvingrove Park alongside. Along the river, the Riverside Museum, Glasgow's museum of transport and travel, is a big hit with families.
